995.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
995.hook: a student begs to be saved, and the teacher answers: fear not, and then, nobody can eat your dinner for you
995.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta the teacher, the guru, is held to be essential for showing the way, while the student is expected to reflect and meditate on the teaching personally until it becomes their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: the qualities a seeker brings, and the surprise that the Vivekachudamani calls seeking your own nature bhakti. What grabbed you, and was it passing? Day nine hundred ninety-five.

The student arrives at the teacher's feet in a state. In the Vivekachudamani he describes himself as scorched, caught in the forest fire of the world, shaken by the winds of misfortune. He has no list of questions ready. He has one request: save me. It's a request that gets carried into doctors' offices and counselors' rooms too. What a teacher says first, in that moment, shapes everything after. The book records it. And then, a little later, it records something harder.
screen: `THE STUDENT ARRIVES SCORCHED.` → `ONE REQUEST: SAVE ME.` → `WHAT DOES THE TEACHER SAY?`

segments.voice: The teacher's first words, in paraphrase: fear not, wise one. There is no danger for you. There is a way across this ocean, the same way the sages crossed, and I will show it to you. That's comfort, plainly given. No lecture on why the student is suffering. Just: you're not lost, there's a road. Then the student finds his questions. What is bondage? How did it come? How does it stay? How do I get free? The teacher praises him for asking. And then comes the harder part. A father in debt, the text says, has sons and others who can pay it off for him. But for bondage, there's no one to free you but yourself. Someone else can lift a heavy load from your head. Hunger, though, goes away only when you eat. A sick person gets well by taking the medicine and keeping to the diet, not by having someone else do it on their behalf. And later the text sharpens it: an illness isn't cured by saying the word medicine, without drinking it. Put the two answers side by side. Fear not, and nobody can do this for you. They sound opposite, but the book holds them together. In the book, the teacher really can show the way, and does. What he can't do is walk it in the student's place. On this path, jnana isn't handed over like a parcel. It has to be eaten, so to speak, by the one who is hungry. That isn't harsh. It's the same respect you give a grown friend: I'll sit with you, and I trust you to stand up.
screen: `FEAR NOT. THERE IS A WAY ACROSS.` · `A DEBT CAN BE PAID BY OTHERS.` · `HUNGER ENDS ONLY WHEN YOU EAT.` · `SAYING MEDICINE DOESN'T CURE.` · then, large: `I'LL SHOW YOU. YOU WALK.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, wherever you're sitting. Bring to mind one thing you've been hoping someone else would fix for you. A worry, a habit, a decision. Hold it lightly. First, let the teacher's words land: fear not, there is a way across. Rest in that for a few breaths. Then ask, without any scolding, what one small step on it is yours alone to take. Don't take it now. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can hold both the comfort and the step together. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani a teacher can show it, but like food or medicine, it works only for the one who takes it.

Your line: jnana, Shankara's Vivekachudamani, selections. Today, catch yourself saying the word for something instead of doing it, and take one small dose of the real thing. Day nine hundred ninety-five.

996.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
996.hook: a bee stays too long inside a lotus, and the petals close at dusk
996.howItsDone: Some students of the Vivekachudamani memorize short verses like this one and recall them during the day, using them to notice where the senses are pulling attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: fear not, there's a way across, and nobody can eat your dinner for you. What small dose of the real thing did you take? Day nine hundred ninety-six.

A bee works its way deep into a lotus on a pond, late in the afternoon, drunk on the scent, and stays. And stays. The light goes gold, then gray. The petals begin to fold inward, slowly, the way lotuses close at evening, and the bee is still inside. The Vivekachudamani puts the bee in a short list of creatures, each one caught by a single sense. Then it turns to the reader and asks a question.
screen: `A BEE INSIDE A LOTUS.` → `THE PETALS CLOSE.` → `A LIST, AND A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. The deer, the elephant, the moth, the fish and the bee: these five die, each bound by one of the five senses, sound, touch, form, taste and smell. What then of a person, bound by all five? The old explanations fill in each picture. The deer is drawn by a hunter's music. The elephant by touch. The moth flies into the flame it can't stop looking at. The fish takes the bait for the taste. And the bee stays in the closing lotus for the smell. Each one is ruined by something good. Music, touch, light, food, fragrance. None of them is evil. That's the sharp edge of the verse. It doesn't say the senses are wicked. It says a creature pulled along by even one of them can lose everything, and asks what happens to someone pulled by all five at once. Notice where this sits in a book about jnana. You might expect a book about knowing to stay in the head. But this verse brings the book right down to the body: what you look at, what you reach for, where your attention gets towed. On this path, discernment isn't only a thought about what lasts. It's noticing, in the moment, which sense has hold of you, and whether you chose it. The moth doesn't decide anything. It just flies. A person can notice the pull before the wings move. That noticing is a small, practical kind of knowing, and the text treats it as part of the road to the larger kind.
screen: `DEER, ELEPHANT, MOTH, FISH, BEE.` · `EACH CAUGHT BY ONE SENSE.` · `WHAT OF ONE CAUGHT BY ALL FIVE?` · `NOTICE THE PULL BEFORE THE WINGS MOVE.` · then, large: `WHICH SENSE HAS HOLD OF YOU?`

segments.voice: Let the body settle. Go through the senses one at a time, slowly, the way the verse lists them. Sound: whatever is in the room. Touch: the weight of the body on the seat. Form: the light behind your eyelids, or the room if your eyes are open. Taste: what's on the tongue right now. Smell: the air. Then ask, quietly, which of these pulls at you most. Don't push it away. Just see it. If you pray, you can offer that sense back as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani it starts small: seeing which sense has hold of you, before it carries you off.

Your line: jnana, Shankara's Vivekachudamani, selections. Today, the next time you reach for your phone, a snack or a song, pause one breath and name the sense that's pulling. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
997.hook: a coil lies across the garden path at dusk, and the Vivekachudamani asks what happens when someone brings a lamp
997.howItsDone: In Advaita teaching, the rope taken for a snake is an image used to explain adhyasa: the Self mistaken for the body and mind, set right by knowing rather than by effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: the bee in the closing lotus, and five creatures each caught by a single sense. Which sense pulled at you? Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

A coil lies across the garden path at dusk. Someone walking home stops dead. The shape is long, it's curved, it might have moved. The heart is pounding now, the breath is short, and the person is already backing toward the gate. Then a neighbor steps out with a lamp. It's a rope. Somebody left it lying there after tying up the gate. Nothing on the path has changed at all. The rope was a rope the whole time. But the fear was real, the pounding was real, and so was the step backward. That small scene on a garden path is a teaching picture on the path of knowing, and the Vivekachudamani puts it to work.
screen: `A COIL ON THE PATH AT DUSK.` → `A LAMP.` → `IT WAS ALWAYS A ROPE.`

segments.voice: When the teacher in the Vivekachudamani wants to show the student what has gone wrong, one picture he reaches for is the rope and the snake. Here's the idea, in paraphrase. Through not knowing, a rope is taken for a snake, and fear follows. Through not knowing, the Self is taken for the body, the mind, the restless one who worries, and suffering follows. The teaching has a name for that mistake: superimposition, adhyasa, laying one thing on top of another. The snake is laid on the rope. The small, anxious I is laid on the Self. Now notice what the cure is not. Nobody kills the snake. Nobody runs for a stick, or a better pair of boots, or a long practice of being brave around snakes. All of that would be fighting something that isn't there. The cure is a lamp. Light falls on the rope, the snake is simply gone, and it doesn't come back as long as the light is on. That's what jnana means on this path. Not collecting facts. Knowing that removes a mistake. And one more thing follows. The rope never needed fixing. It was never in danger. On this reading, the Self was never actually bound; the binding belonged to the seeing. That's why, as we heard two days ago, the teacher insists the student must look for themselves. A lamp held by someone else helps. But the snake only disappears for the one whose own eyes see the rope.
screen: `A ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `ADHYASA: ONE THING LAID ON ANOTHER.` · `NOBODY KILLS THE SNAKE.` · `THE CURE IS A LAMP.` · then, large: `THE ROPE NEVER NEEDED FIXING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Before long a thought will arrive dressed as a fact about you: I'm tired, I'm behind, I'm not good at this. When one comes, don't argue with it and don't chase it off. Just hold a small lamp to it. Notice that it's a thought, appearing, and notice what is aware of it appearing. The thought may stay or go. Either way, keep the light on and keep looking. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing, on the path of knowing: not a pile of facts, but the seeing that turns the snake back into a rope.
Your line: jnana, Shankara's Vivekachudamani, in selections. Today, when something sets the heart pounding, ask once: is this a snake, or a rope in poor light? Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

998.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
998.hook: an arrow is already flying when the archer sees the tiger was a cow
998.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers often explain the jivanmukta, the one free while living, through prarabdha karma: actions already begun play out in the body's life, while knowledge ends the mistaken sense of being bound by them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: a rope taken for a snake, and the lamp that ends the fear without a fight. Did anything turn out to be a rope? Today, our last day in the Vivekachudamani. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

An archer at the edge of a field sees a striped shape in the long grass. A tiger. He draws and lets the arrow go. And in the half second after it leaves the string, the shape lifts its head. It's a cow. The archer knows the truth now, completely. But the arrow is already in the air. Knowing can't call it back. It will land where it was aimed. The Vivekachudamani tells this little story late in the book, and it uses it to answer a hard question. If knowing sets someone free, why does the free person still have a body, still get hungry, still catch a cold?
screen: `A STRIPED SHAPE IN THE GRASS.` → `THE ARROW IS ALREADY FLYING.` → `WHY DOES THE FREE ONE STILL CATCH COLDS?`

segments.voice: The text's answer, in paraphrase, runs like this. Actions already set in motion before knowing dawns are like that arrow. Their name is prarabdha, the karma that has already begun. Knowing doesn't stop them. They play out, and the body that came with them lives on until they're spent. What knowing does stop is the next arrow. The person who sees clearly no longer draws the bow from fear, from grabbing, from the old mistake about who they are. So the Vivekachudamani describes someone it calls jivanmukta, free while living. Not a ghost, not a statue. A person who eats and sleeps and walks to the market, the way everyone does. The difference is inside. The text compares it to waking from a dream. In the dream there was a palace, a debt, a chase down a hallway. On waking, none of it binds. The dream may have been vivid, but nobody wakes up and pays the dream's debts. That's how the free one holds the body's life, the book says: lightly, as something seen, not something that defines them. The text then adds a qualifier: prarabdha holds only while someone takes themselves to be the body. For the one who knows, it says, even that falls away. Here our selections come into one view. A student arrives desperate to be free. A teacher shows that the binding was a mistake, a rope taken for a snake. The cure is knowing, jnana. And the one who knows still lives an ordinary life, with the old arrows landing one by one, and no new ones drawn. Some readers find that ending a relief. On this account, freedom doesn't mean a life with no weather in it. It means not mistaking the weather for yourself.
screen: `PRARABDHA: THE ARROW ALREADY FLYING.` · `KNOWING STOPS THE NEXT ARROW.` · `JIVANMUKTA: FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `LIKE WAKING FROM A DREAM.` · then, large: `NO NEW ARROWS DRAWN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the body settle. Notice whatever the body is carrying right now: an ache, tiredness, a full stomach, a restless foot. Treat each one as an arrow already in flight. It will land; let it. You don't need to fix it or follow it. Then watch the mind for the next arrow, the reaction that wants to be drawn: a complaint, a plan, a worry. Notice it, and leave the bow where it is. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing that frees: it can't call back the arrows already flying, but it stops drawing new ones.

Your line: jnana, Shankara's Vivekachudamani, in selections. Today, when something old lands on you, a bill, a mood, a consequence, let it land, and notice whether you're drawing a new arrow in reply. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

999.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
999.hook: a king asks three questions in one breath, and a sage answers without offering him a single thing to do
999.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita is read and studied by students of Advaita Vedanta, often slowly with a teacher, and some recite or chant its Sanskrit verses; it is a dialogue in which King Janaka asks and the sage Ashtavakra answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana, and the end of the Vivekachudamani: the arrow already flying, and the one who is free while living. Did an old arrow land on you? Today, a new book on the same path. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

Before the book there's a boy, and the Mahabharata tells his story. While still in his mother's womb, it says, he heard his father reciting the sacred texts and spoke up to correct him. The father, stung, cursed the child, and the boy was born bent in eight places. So he was called Ashtavakra, eight bends. Later, still young, he walked into the court of King Janaka of Videha and out-argued the court's champion in debate. The book named for him, the Ashtavakra Gita, takes that pairing and puts them in a quieter room. Just the sage and the king. And the king opens with a question.
screen: `A BOY WHO CORRECTED HIS FATHER.` → `BORN BENT IN EIGHT PLACES.` → `A SAGE AND A KING, ALONE.`

segments.voice: Janaka's first words, in paraphrase, are three questions in one breath. How is knowledge gained? How does freedom come? How is detachment reached? It's the question of a busy man who wants a method. A teacher might hand him a program: these practices, in this order, for this long. Ashtavakra's first answer sounds like ethics. If you want freedom, my child, he says, leave the objects of the senses as you'd leave poison, and drink forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth as you'd drink nectar. Then he turns sharply. You aren't earth, he says, or water, or fire, or air, or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these, consciousness itself. And then, a verse later, the turn that gives this book its edge. If you set the body aside and simply rest in awareness, he says, you are happy, at peace and free of bondage, right now. Not after the practices. Not at the end of the road. Now. That's how the Ashtavakra Gita reads. It hardly gives instructions. It keeps pointing at what the king already is, and asking him to notice. Over these six days we'll walk through it in large steps, not verse by verse: the king's question, a line about bondage and freedom, the king's own awakening, the sage testing him, a chapter about forgetting everything, and the last chapter's long litany. Some readers find it too abrupt to use. Others find that abruptness is the whole gift. It doesn't ask Janaka to become something new. It asks him to stop overlooking what's already here.
screen: `THREE QUESTIONS IN ONE BREATH.` · `POISON AND NECTAR.` · `NOT EARTH, WATER, FIRE, AIR OR SPACE.` · `THE WITNESS, FREE NOW.` · then, large: `NOT AFTER THE ROAD. NOW.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Notice the body: its weight, its warmth, the floor beneath it. Notice sounds in the room, and the thoughts drifting through. Then, gently, notice the noticing itself, the awareness in which the body, the sounds and the thoughts all show up. There's no need to push anything away. Just rest there, as the one who sees. The bell holds the time.
The Ashtavakra Gita: a conversation between a sage and King Janaka, which points at freedom as something to notice rather than something to earn.
Your line: the Ashtavakra Gita, complete. Today, between two tasks, take one breath to notice the one who is noticing, before you pick up the next thing. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

1000.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1000.hook: one verse says the one who takes themselves to be free is free, and the one who takes themselves to be bound is bound
1000.howItsDone: Students of the Ashtavakra Gita often memorize or recite individual verses in Sanskrit, and the verse on being free or bound is one that teachers quote when discussing how bondage, on this view, lies in identification rather than in the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita began: King Janaka's three questions, and a sage who answered, rest as the witness, free now. Did you catch the one who notices? Day one thousand.

Free, if you take yourself as free. Bound, if you take yourself as bound. That's the line, in paraphrase, from the first chapter of the Ashtavakra Gita. And the sage adds something odd. He doesn't present it as his own discovery. He says it's a saying people repeat, and that this saying is true: as the mind holds itself, so it goes. It's a strange thing to hear on the thousandth day of anything. A thousand days of practice could make a person feel they're finally getting somewhere, or that they still have miles to go. This verse would quietly ask about both: who is doing the counting?
screen: `FREE, IF YOU TAKE YOURSELF AS FREE.` → `A SAYING, AND IT'S TRUE.` → `WHO IS DOING THE COUNTING?`

segments.voice: Read quickly, the verse sounds like a poster on a gym wall. Believe in yourself and anything is possible. But in the Ashtavakra Gita it means something stranger, and the verses around it show why. A few verses earlier, the sage tells Janaka that bondage is this one thing: seeing someone else as the seer, rather than yourself. Then he says the king has been bitten by the black snake of egoism, the thought, I am the doer. Drink the nectar of faith, he says, in the thought, I am not the doer, and be happy. And then comes the line. One who holds that they're free is free. One who holds that they're bound is bound. So the verse isn't about positive thinking. It's not saying, think hard enough and you'll get a better life. It's saying the binding was never in the world. It was in the taking, in what consciousness took itself to be. Ashtavakra's word for free is mukta. On his account, a person doesn't build their way to mukta. They stop insisting they're bound. A thousand days into this path, that cuts both ways, and the text wouldn't mind. The days of practice are real. The sitting, the reading, the lamps and the songs are real. But this book would say the one who sat for all of them was never in a cell to begin with. On its account, freedom is not a reward at the end of a long climb. It's a fact about the climber, available on day one, and on day one thousand.
screen: `NOT A POSTER ON A GYM WALL.` · `BITTEN BY THE SNAKE OF I AM THE DOER.` · `THE BINDING WAS IN THE TAKING.` · `MUKTA: FREE.` · then, large: `A FACT ABOUT THE CLIMBER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath move on its own. Notice the sense of being the one who is doing all this: sitting, breathing, trying. Then try the sage's small turn. Let the breath breathe itself, with no one pulling it in or pushing it out. Let sounds arrive without anyone needing to hear them. If the thought I'm doing this comes back, notice it as one more thought passing through. The bell holds the time.
The Ashtavakra Gita, and its line on freedom: free if you take yourself as free, bound if you take yourself as bound. The binding lives in the taking.
Your line: the Ashtavakra Gita, complete. Today, once, when you catch yourself saying I'm stuck, ask quietly who is taking themselves to be stuck. Day one thousand.

1001.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1001.hook: in chapter two the student stops asking and starts exclaiming, and the king bows to himself
1001.howItsDone: In the Ashtavakra Gita, chapter two is Janaka's response, and students reading the text with a teacher often treat it as a picture of what the sage's teaching sounds like once it lands: wonder rather than argument.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita and its line on freedom: free if you take yourself as free, bound if you take yourself as bound. This week ran from the Vivekachudamani's bee, rope and arrow into the Ashtavakra Gita. Did you catch anyone insisting on being stuck? Day one thousand one.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `THE BINDING LIVES IN THE TAKING.`

segments.voice: Aho. It's a Sanskrit cry of wonder, the sound someone makes when a thing turns out to be bigger than expected. And it's how King Janaka opens the second chapter. In the first chapter he asked his three questions and listened. Now the teacher falls silent and the student speaks, and he doesn't ask anything at all. He exclaims. A few verses in, what comes out of his mouth is surprising enough to make a first-time reader look twice. He bows to himself.
screen: `AHO: A CRY OF WONDER.` → `THE STUDENT STOPS ASKING.` → `THE KING BOWS TO HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's how chapter two begins, in paraphrase. Aho, I am spotless, at peace, pure awareness, beyond nature. All this time I've been fooled by delusion. Then Janaka reaches for the sea. As waves and foam and bubbles are nothing other than water, he says, so this whole world, flowing out of the Self, is nothing other than the Self. A wave can rise high or crash on the rocks, and it never stops being water. Then come the verses that make people sit up. Wonderful am I, Janaka says. Salutation to me. Namo mahyam. I remain, he says, even when the whole world, from the creator down to a blade of grass, is destroyed. On the surface that sounds like a king who has had too much praise. But the I in these verses isn't the king. It isn't Janaka with a crown and a treasury. It's the awareness he was pointed to on the first day, the witness. When he bows to that, he's bowing to what he takes to be in everything, including the blade of grass. The line between the two is fine, and the text walks it. On this reading, the small I that wants credit is exactly what has dropped away. What's left can't be flattered, because there's no one left to flatter. That's why the chapter sounds like joy and not like vanity. A man who thought he was a wave has just found out he's water. And what he does with the discovery is not explain it. He sings.
screen: `SPOTLESS, AT PEACE, PURE AWARENESS.` · `WAVES, FOAM AND BUBBLES ARE WATER.` · `NAMO MAHYAM: SALUTATION TO ME.` · `NOT THE KING. THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `THE WAVE FINDS IT'S WATER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Notice the thoughts and feelings rising and falling like waves: a plan, a memory, a flicker of worry. Don't try to calm them. Just watch each one rise, and watch it sink back. Then notice what they rise in, the awareness itself, the water under the waves. If a wave seems big, let it be big. It's still water. The bell holds the time.
The Ashtavakra Gita, chapter two: the king's cry of wonder, and the waves that were water all along.
Your line: the Ashtavakra Gita, complete. Today, when a strong mood rises, name it a wave once, out loud or under your breath, and watch it come back down. Day one thousand one.
